content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a knowledge distillation method to transfer knowledge from large DETR to small DETR. The proposed method is composed of three parts: teacher-assisted assignment distillation, attention-agnostic feature distillation and progressive instance distillation. Extensive results on MSCOCO show the effectiveness of the proposed knowledge distillation method. Ablation studies are provided to clarify the importance of each of three parts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
As it is very time-consuming and memory-consuming to train DETR, thereby knowledge distillation might be one solution to re-use large DETR with no re-training from scratch. The proposed knowledge distillation method considers the characteristics in DETR and integrates three knowledge distillation objectives at difference positions of the DETR architecture. Experimental results show the small DETR can achieve competitive performance with the large one via using the proposed method. Several concerns about the paper are:

-- The novelty in the proposed knowledge distillation method is limited, as all the loss objectives are similar to previous methods. In addition, the three distillation parts (teacher-assisted assignment distillation, attention-agnostic feature distillation and progressive instance distillation) consist of some loss terms, leading to a more complex training optimization. Moreover, the experiments lack of discussions on the weights of the loss terms.

-- The attention-agnostic feature distillation lacks a clear motivation. It is encouraged to clarify more on its insights and advantages over existing feature distillation manners.

-- In teacher-assisted assignment distillation, it is unclear how to compute the loss cost based on Eq.(10)(11).

-- In the experiments, it is encouraged to show the training and inference time between Teacher and Student, apart from the accuracy performance. In addition, is it possible to train the student with more epochs for better accuracy?

-- Although MS COCO is the most widely used benchmark, it is interesting to see more results on other object detection datasets.

-- In Table 2, we can see each of the three distillation terms can achieve about 1\% boosts compared with the baseline. Unfortunately, combining all of the three terms can bring about 2\% boosts instead of 3\%. It implies the three terms should have some positive and negative interactions. It lacks more insightful analysis on these results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is organized clearly with comprehensive details.
It should be possible to reproduce the reported results in the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper presents many technical details, even though the overall novelty is weak somewhat.
It is interesting to see the reply from the authors for the questions above.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method for distilling larger (backbone & number of queries) DETR-style models into smaller DETR-style models. The proposed method consists of several components / losses, efficacy and importance of which is studied through extension experiment on COCO with ResNet backbones. The method is shown to perform favourable when compared to prior approaches.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
* Well-written and well-motivated paper on an important topic. As DETR-style models are becoming better and increasingly more popular distilling the large best-performing models into more light-weight ones becomes very important for practical applications.
* The paper carefully ablates various components of the proposed method, verifying that all of them are important.
* Experimental results on COCO show that the model performs well in practice.

**Weaknesses**
* The definition of DETR-family models used in the paper is rather narrow. For example, the authors assume that the model will always have a decoder, where decoder-less models that reply on bipartite matching are also used in practice.
* Restricting experiments to ResNet architectures is also somewhat limiting. More recent DETR-style models (e.g. OWL-ViT) use transformer-based backbones.
* One aspect besides model size that is very important but not considered in the paper is the input image resolution. For example, is it possible to distill a DETR performing well on a 1024px input resolution into a DETR that runs on 256px resolution? This would provide immense computational cost savings, especially for transformer-based backbones.
* The distillation method is somewhat complex - consisting of a larger number of losses (and thus hyper-paramteres) that are used for distillation.
* Minor: "[...] prove the universality [...] of our method" - experiments on COCO with one type of backbone do not *prove* universality.
* Minor: "By pushing the query features between unmatched pairs, we can also provide explicit supervision to prevent repeated prediction." Makes me think that this loss is doing more than just distillation. Is that correct? If so, please be explicit about this in the paper.
* Minor: In Table 1 it looks like for DDETR your method performs better than the teacher model by ~2AP points. How is that possible?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clearly written paper. Experiments should be reproducible if code is published.
content.summary_of_the_review: Interesting work that would be more impactful with additional experimental validation. Some claims in the paper are a bit too strong.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper attempts to tackle the problem of knowledge distillation for the fashional transformer-based detectors. The proposed DETRDistill consists of three main parts, namely the progressive stage-by-stage instance distillation, the attention-agnostic feature distillation and the teacher-assisted assignment distillation. The experiments shown in the paper evidence the effectiveness of the proposed KD.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
+ Interesting topic. The authors attempt to conduct the knowledge distillation for transformer-based detectors, which is novel and interesting.

+ Experiments and ablation studies with AdaMixer and Deformable DETR show the effectiveness of the proposed knowledge distillation framework.

**Weaknesses**

However, there are still some concerns to be addressed:

- Overall, the manuscript is somehow hard to understand with some strange words. It is better to invite a native speaker to revise the whole paper. For example,

	- The citations are not in a good format, e.g. "Dai et al. (Zhu et al., 2020) proposed Deformable DETR...", "(Hinton et al., 2015) first ...".

	- $M$, $N$, and $\phi$ are used multiple times.

- As for the progressive instance distillation, it is limited to the case where the number of stages is the same for teacher and student. However, how to use it if they are different? 

-  As for the attention-agnostic feature distillation, to my understanding, it tries to match the features and relations of the queries. Then, what is the eq5 for? To me it is useless, and so does Figure 2 shown here. What do $\sigma(i)$ and $i$ here stand for? Moreover, this method also limits to the cases where the queries of the teacher and student have the same dimension. How does eq7 hold when the number of queries is different? 

- As for the teacher-assisted assignment distillation, the trained queries from teacher models are used for training the student. An alternative could be initializing the student queries by the teacher queries when it possible, which could be included in the ablation study.

- The results with the previous FGD, MGD etc. are quite worse even compared to the baseline. It is not quite clear how to adapt them in the transformer-based detector knowledge distillation. Could you please clarify this?

- The main claim of the paper is a bit overstated. First of all, it is hard to say the proposed KD pipeline is "simple". This paper only works with 2 models in DETR-families, which is not sufficient. More experiments and discussions on other efficient DETR models, such as ViDT[A], could further support the claims.


**Minor comments**

It is worth discussing a related work [B], in which both the classification and localization are improved via specific distillation strategies. It is interesting to the research line of KD in object detection.

**Reference**

[A] Song. et al. ViDT: An Efficient and Effective Fully Transformer-based Object Detector. ICLR2022

[B] Guo. et al. Distilling Image Classifiers in Object Detectors. NeurIPS2021

Novelty: Fair. The topic is interesting, but the method is a stack of previous methods.

Reproducibility: Fair. No supplementary code.

Because the paper claims the contribution to the transformer-based detectors family, to this end, the experiments only with 2 models are not quite sufficient.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new knowledge distillation method dedicated to DETR families. The proposed method adopts progressive instance distillation,  attention-agnostic feature distillation, and teacher-assisted assignment distillation to boost the performance of the light student model. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**:
* DETR brings in new properties against previous CNN-based detectors. And it is important to explore knowledge distillation on DETR families. The proposed DETRDistill is reasonable to boost the distillation performance of the light DETR-style student model.
* The proposed method demonstrates better experimental performance than previous state-of-the-art knowledge distillation on two DETR-style detectors (AdaMixer and Deformable DETR).

**Weaknesses**
* There are also some prior methods that explore distillation on DETR-style detectors[2], which have not been discussed and cited in the related work. What is the difference between the proposed DETRDistill and [1]?
* I do not quite understand how teacher queries $Q^T$ guide the optimization of students' *Decoder* and *FFN*. $\hat{y}^T$ in Eq. (11) is predicted through the student's module and teacher's queries. However, $Q^T$ is learned embeddings of the teacher, which is fixed in the teacher model during distillation and only produces stable and precise results through the teacher's module. So can authors quantitatively validate the stability in Hungarian match with the posed stable queries $Q^T$.
* This paper mainly utilizes the queries of the teacher to guide the distillation. So what is the similarity between students' queries and teachers' queries in latent space? 
* This paper only investigates distillation on encoder-decoder DETR-style detectors. The effectiveness on the encoder-only DETR-style detector, such as YOLOS [2], is unknown.

[1] Song, Hwanjun et al. “ViDT: An Efficient and Effective Fully Transformer-based Object Detector.” ArXiv abs/2110.03921 (2022): n. pag.

[2] Fang, Yuxin et al. “You Only Look at One Sequence: Rethinking Transformer in Vision through Object Detection.” NeurIPS (2021).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* **Clarity**: most contents are clear and easy to follow.
* **Quality**: The proposed method is evaluated on the COCO benchmark and shows better performance than previous methods.
* **Novelty**: The design principles have some in common with previous methods, but some details are new.
* **Reproducibility**: Most implementation details are provided but the code is not available.
content.summary_of_the_review: The overall idea is good while the main concerns lie in the demonstration of assignment distillation and insufficient experiments and discussions with the previous related method.

content.title: DETRDistill: A Simple Knowledge Distillation Framework for DETR-Families
content.abstract: Transformer-based detectors (DETRs) have attracted great attention due to their sparse training paradigm and the removal of post-processing operations, but the huge model can be computationally time-consuming and difficult to be deployed in real-world applications. To tackle this problem, knowledge distillation (KD) can be employed to compress the huge model by constructing a simple teacher-student learning framework. Different from the traditional CNN detectors, where the distillation targets can be naturally aligned through the feature map, DETR regards object detection as a set prediction problem, leading to an unclear relationship between teacher and student during distillation. In this paper, we propose DETRDistill, a novel knowledge distillation dedicated to DETR-families. We first explore a sparse matching paradigm with progressive stage-by-stage instance distillation. Considering the diverse attention mechanisms adopted in different DETRs, we propose attention-agnostic feature distillation module to overcome the ineffectiveness of conventional feature imitation. Finally, to fully leverage the intermediate products from the teacher, we introduce teacher-assisted assignment distillation, which greatly alleviates the instability of label assignment caused by bipartite graph matching. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our distillation method achieves significant improvement on various competitive DETR approaches, without introducing extra consumption in the inference phase. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study to explore a general distillation method for DETR-style detectors.
